Recently, our group introduced LEAD, a neural network framework designed to encode data streams with a near 100% precision rate, functioning as a source coder. LEAD's architecture leverages two primary components: a variational auto-encoder (VAE) responsible for generating codes and a zero-error module that refines them into final outputs. In this paper, we adopt a graph-theoretic approach to examine how these codes are error-corrected to achieve zero bit error rates. Furthermore, through a theoretical analysis, this framework reveals an interesting finding: when codes are generated using a standard VAE, increasing the model's capacity often degrades the overall performance of the resulting source encoding. Consequently, an optimal balance must be identified to select the number of VAE parameters. In this search for optimal configurations, this study identifies two distinct forms of information leakage that can negatively impact performance: (i) a prior leakage, in which non-optimal prior distributions allow reconstruction errors to persist; and (ii) an encoder leakage, in which specific data patterns cause the encoder to produce erroneous code words. Based on this analysis, several practical guidelines are provided to assist in selecting LEAD's hyperparameters with greater confidence.

Deep generative models have proven highly effective for satellite image synthesis, yet significant hurdles remain in their application to Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery. SAR data is characterized by extreme speckle noise, which causes inconsistent patterns in both background and targets, thereby complicating generalization and statistical analysis. Additionally, classifying and detecting objects in SAR scenes is difficult due to limited radiometric details and pronounced geometric distortions, even as multi-scale SAR acquisition offers only a singular high-resolution option. To address these bottlenecks, this paper proposes MrSARP, a novel hierarchical deep generative model designed to create High-Resolution (HR) SAR images from Low-Resolution (LR) inputs. The architecture utilizes an encoder-decoder framework where both components are SAR-specific, extracted features leverage discriminative priors, and the generator synthesizes HR data through multi-stage upscaling. Crucially, a dedicated classifier module, adapted to SAR characteristics, acts as a regularization mechanism to boost generation quality by integrating hierarchical hierarchical loss derived from accurate predictions. Extensive experimental validation confirms that the proposed method surpasses general-purpose models, including general-purpose general-purpose models, in recovering SAR multi-scale structures and outperforms existing techniques in recovering multi-scale structures and exceeds standard general-purpose models.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) represents an approach using near-term variational quantum hardware to tackle combinatorial optimization challenges. Despite its potential, OQA faces inherent hurdles related to the difficulty of parameter estimation through noisy and limited measurements, as well as issues with getting stuck in poor local optima. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a method for Bayesian optimization of QAOA that runs concurrently with the algorithm itself. By utilizing the collected data from QAOA runs, the accompanying optimization procedure constructs a surrogate model of the objective function, enabling the Bayesian acquisition function to explore the parameter landscape more intelligently. This co-occurrence strategy offers several distinct advantages over standard techniques: it dramatically lowers the number of hardware circuit evaluations needed per outer optimization iteration, facilitates parallel execution with QAOA, and mitigates reliance on gradient approximations that can prove inaccurate within noisy environments. Empirical results demonstrate that, across representative test cases for graph problems like Max-Cut and Minimum Vertex Cover, this Bayesian optimization strategy outperforms conventional methods by delivering higher quality solutions while significantly cutting down on communication overhead between the quantum processor and the classical controller.

This paper addresses the determination of pairwise intersections among ellipse sets, yielding a partitioning of the plane comprising an outer ellipse set encased by an intricate arrangement of interior ellipsites. We present an algorithm capable of computing the partition's constituent elements. Specifically, we analyze the complexity of this geometry: the outer set is defined by the ellipsites with external boundaries, while the internal structure results from shared edges and vertices among all intersecting pairs. We demonstrate that the vertex count is proportional to the square of the ellipse set size. Additionally, each set's representation is reduced to quadratic relative to the total set count. Consequently, any algorithmic method for generating the planar partition operates within quadratic time and space complexity. We utilize V\'{e}en's Theorem to establish these vertex time limits and subsequently apply coordinate scaling techniques to validate the proposed algorithms.

Continual learning addresses the issue of traditional batch learning systems that must retain past training data when processing new information streams. A novel approach known as "q-Training" allows neural networks to adapt to this ongoing flow of data without needing to remember previous examples. By introducing a parameter q into the input of a convolutional layer, this technique enables the creation of localized structures that change over time. These regions depend on the value of q and their spatial positions are continuously re-optimized for every new dataset. Because a fresh dataset typically covers a broader range of q-q pairs, these dynamic regions effectively replace the need to store historical data, allowing the memory system to remain current. This method has been tested and proven on artificial problems, including Gaussian Mixture Distinguishability and the de-aliasing of MNIST digits, as well as on major computer vision benchmarks like CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CIFAR-10.

The mechanism driving magnetism in triangular lattice systems, such as $\mathrm{Fe}_5\mathrm{Ge}_2$, remains a subject of debate, with both frustration-induced fluctuating moments and classical short-range order proposed. This study utilizes $\mathbf{k}$-space Hubbard model analysis at half-filling to investigate the low-temperature ferromagnetic (FM) and antiferromagnetic (AFM) instabilities. We find that an almost negligible interplanar hopping $t'$ is essential for the nearest-neighbor Heisenberg AFM exchange to dominate, whereas a larger $t'$ drives a nearest-neighbor ferrimagnetic $1/3$ holon instability. Our findings support the role of quantum disorder (order-by-disorders) in generating short-range AFM states, while also demonstrating that long-range magnetic order depends heavily on structural distortions.

Gathered within a single image or slice, vertebral recognition is a core challenge in medical diagnostics with broad applications, ranging from organ localization to image registration. Yet extractingu verteae from the intricate complexities of abdominal regions remains arduous due to distracting artifacts caused by noise, calcium deposits, and soft tissue. This study introduces a deep autoencoder framework designed to automatically position and identify vertebrae in CT scans. The system first rectifies the spine to align vertebrae horizontally or vertically within each slice. Subsequently, an anatomical constraint guides a focused enhancement process to isolate the vertebral region from background clutter. Finally, the framework employs a classifier to identify the vertebrae present. Evaluated across 350 slices sourced from the Corion-3D CT dataset, the algorithm achieved high recognition accuracy of 93.6% and achieved average precision and precision scores of 90.1% and 87.6%, respectively.

In stochastic processes, fluctuation theorems illuminate rare trajectory properties by relying on the assumption that the time-reversed process shares an asymptotic rate function with original process. However, this assumption fails when analyzing time-averaged currents within finite time scales under conditions of energy conservation violations. We address this issue by extending the method developed in reference [B. Doyon and J. R. Speck, Phys. Rev. Lett. 114, 220601 (2015)] to incorporate time scales finite relative to system size, thereby enabling the derivation of exact symmetry relations for the asymptotic distribution of scaled quantities. We apply this method generally and demonstrate its utility through a billiard system involving current operators that fail to commute with the Hamiltonian but become effectively commuting in the large-cutoff limit. Our approach yields a $\Lambda$-gauge-invariant asymptotic distribution of such current operators. We note that this gauge invariance arises because the current operators approach the system's energy eigenbasis as the limit is taken. These findings establish a necessary foundation for subsequent research aimed at proving fluctuation theorems for fine-grained operators within finite durations.

Riganti's recent findings demonstrate that the relative quantum homology of $T^* \text{Quot}^h(\mathbb{C}^m, \mathbb{C}^n, \mathbb{C}^n)$$ relative to two $K$-polystable tori is generated by two $K$-polystable tori. In this study, we extend these results to the broader class of rational maps $f\,:\,\mathbb{C}^m,\rightarrow\,\mathbb{C}^n$, where the relative quantum homology of the $K$-polystable tori mapping kernel is demonstrated to be $K$-polystable tori mapping kernel. We also provide an explicit decomposition of the relative quantum homomorphism of such symplectic quotients into a relative homomorphism of the $K$-polystable tori mapping quotient components of the relative morphism.

Piezo crystals are commonly utilized as resonators in which acoustic wave propagation is restricted. However, this study demonstrates that a pair of properly oriented and positioned crystals can achieve the complete transmission of acoustic waves. We demonstrate this effect by using a Scanning Acoustic Microscope to observe waves traveling within a quartz crystal when a second quartz crystal acts as their termination. By adjusting the crystals' orientation and separation distance, fully transmissive states are realized, enabling the entire input acoustic power to pass through. theoretical modeling supports these observations by confirming that constructive coupling between the crystals leads to transmission states characterized by the spatial localization of acoustic energy. These findings suggest new applications in piezoelectric systems, offering a pathway to confine, manipulate, and propagate acoustic waves within nanosized piezoelectric structures.

Particle dynamics within reservoirs are typically governed by random forces and spatially inhomogeneous potential fields, resulting in highly structured self-generated phase spaces that exhibit a complex mosaic of regions characterized by either trapped dynamics or ballistic transport. Despite this complexity, global statistical properties are often determined solely by the reservoir parameters, largely ignoring the intricate geometry of these phase spaces. Conversely, this complex geometric landscape can fully express itself through low-dimensional quantum entities such as exciton-polaritons. We propose organizing a quantum fluid composed of exciton-polaritons across an extensive reservoir to map the fluid's emergent characteristics—specifically its geometry and topology—directly onto the statistical behavior of individual particles. Consequently, this setup enables a novel form of topological counting utilizing quantum critical fluctuations to reveal the quantum expression of a classical environment.

Our latest observations utilizing the Gran Telescopio Canarias with the Multi-object Infrared Spectrograph and Camera provide high-resolution spectra of the giant planet, revealing definitive evidence of a massive dust envelope. Analysis of broad emission features associated with silicate features (11.28 µm), oxycarbonates (13.02 µm), and oxycarbonates (15.92 µm) confirms their presence. This article presents Daany, a .NET-based data analysis framework. It is designed to offer both a programming library and a Service-Oriented Architecture, enabling the creation of RESTful services powered by SQL and NoSQL datastore operations.

This paper examines the 1612 Galileo vs. Redini controversy within the context of the early 17th century, a pivotal era where mathematics was gradually gaining dominance over philosophy in driving scientific progress. The article highlights a fundamental disagreement between the two thinkers: Galileo held that mathematics held supremacy over nature in terms of exactness, whereas Redini argued that philosophical truth was more reliable because it resisted simplification by abstract generalizations, thereby offering a more comprehensive understanding of actual reality despite being less precise. Furthermore, the document addresses the common misconception that the 17th century represented an unalloyed celebration of mathematics in science, noting instead the coexistence of skeptics, such as Redini, who sought to check the growing arrogance of scholars who claimed every aspect of nature could be elucidated through the "golden key" of mathematical reasoning.

A novel hybrid model featuring dynamically integrated Particle-in-cell (PIC) and Magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) simulations was employed to investigate magnetic island merging. This approach accurately captures both nonlinear reconnection processes and post-merging hydrodynamic behaviors. Using initial configurations of two elongated magnetic flux ropes separated by a current sheet, the study examined how varying parameters influence the timing of merge events and the characteristics resulting from them. Specifically, analyses focused on how changes to MHD parameters affected key metrics—including collapse rate, expansion velocity, final kinetic energy, and magnetic reconnection rate—following the collapse. While MHD alone tends to overlook the intricate kinetic details inherent in these phenomena, the proposed hybrid technique successfully bridges this gap by resolving both energy and entropy, offering a comprehensive understanding of the physical mechanisms involved.

Current code-generation models, trained on vast datasets to produce functional programs, are becoming standard tools for developers. However, applying these models effectively requires users to skillfully craft prompts that elicit correct code, often requiring significant adaptation to each tool's specific behavioral quirks. We introduce **Amanuensis**, a version tailored to streamline this experience by adopting a "guided drafting" strategy. Drawing an analogy to a writer with an amanuensis—a personal secretary who drafts text on their behalf—Amanuensis functions as a programming assistant that closely mirrors its user's intent.

By initially generating only short, incremental snippets based on the user's input, the system subsequently refines them into complete programs. This process effectively acts as an internal code-review step, allowing the model to verify logic and catch errors before finalizing the output. Evaluation against state-of-the-art alternatives indicates that Amansuensis not only generates code with greater functional correctness but also does so with fewer hallucinations. Furthermore, users find that this tool saves more time than competing programs-assistants.
